newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries up after Fed holds line on rates.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries up after Fed holds line on rates.

text.p: Treasury securities ended moderately higher Tuesday after the Federal Reserve surprised the market by not raising interest rates.

A rate hike was widely expected as recent wage gains and a low unemployment rate were seen as forerunners of inflation that would persuade Fed officials to raise rates at Tuesday's much anticipated policy meeting.

In the half hour before the Fed said its policy-making Federal Open Market Committee had left rates untouched, bond prices climbed about one-third of a point from levels that had been nearly unchanged on the day.
After the announcement, the market doubled that gain, before conceding a good portion of it.
The bellwether 30-year Treasury bond closed 14/32 higher, reducing its yield to 6.99 percent from 7.02 percent at Monday's close.
"The knee jerk reaction was the simple one in which the market rallied to news that rates are going to be held steady for a time," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
"But then prices backed down from their peaks on the thought that the Fed is doing experiments with inflation and that it's not as vigilant on inflation as perhaps it should be."

Short-term bill rates, which are most responsive to near-term Fed policy adjustments, fell sharply as prospects for higher official interest rates receded at least until the Fed's next policy meeting in November, analysts said.
Three- and six-month Treasury bill rates fell 20 basis points and 14 basis points, respectively, closing at 4.97 percent and 5.15 percent.
"You'll be dealing with a 5-1/4 percent Federal funds rate until November at the earliest," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

At 5.25 percent currently, the fed funds rate -- charged by banks with excess reserves at a Fed district bank to banks needing overnight loans -- is the most sensitive indicator of the direction of interest rates.

Samuel Kahan, president of A.S.K. Financial Research Ltd., said the Fed had relied on "the basic assumption that the economic numbers are suffiently mixed that a case can be made for the economy's moderation in the future."
Kahan said the Fed may also have decided to hold rates steady because inflation has not accelerated.
Elliott Platt, managing director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, said the big risk to the market now would be stronger-than-anticipated economic data.
Platt said he expected upcoming reports on durable goods orders, new home sales and September payroll growth to be subdued, adding anything contrary to that would set the market back, he said.

"That's the big risk," Platt said. "Let's say the September payrolls report is strong and the next CPI is up 0.3 percent. The market could have a horrible case of indigestion which would have been mitigated by some sort of pre-emptive rate hike by the Fed. But the Fed apparently thinks it's a risk worth taking."

At the close, the year bill rate fell 12 basis points to 5.40 percent. The two-year note was up 6/32 to 99-31/32, yielding 6.14 percent, the five-year note up 12/32 at 99-31/32, yielding 6.51 percent and the 10-year note up 15/32 at 101-24/32 to yield 6.75 percent.
